fixes.explanation: Yes, friend. “Even if He causes grief, He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion.” Grief is real in this poem, and the writer says so out loud. But compassion follows right in the same verse.

Yes. “Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has ordained it?” I once told a hot batch to cool faster, and that batch ignored me completely. The writer's answer is right in the question: the Lord.

Yes. “Do not both adversity and good come from the mouth of the Most High?” The writer puts adversity and good side by side in one question. I think that's him saying both out loud, with no tiptoeing. That's why the blank is good.
Right on. The word is “Your,” not “His,” so he's speaking straight to the LORD. Verse 22 talks about Him, and verse 23 turns and talks to Him. That little shift is easy to miss, so nice catch, baker.
Yes, friend. The soul says, “The LORD is my portion…” and then adds, “therefore I will hope in Him.” A portion is a share, the piece that's yours. And the soul says that piece is the LORD.
A king is a natural guess when a heavy load shows up, friend. But no king appears in this verse. The writer says, “…for the LORD has laid it upon him.” That's the name that fills the blank.

Yes, friend. “Even if He causes grief, He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion.” Grief is real in this poem, and the writer says so out loud. But compassion follows right in the same verse.

A king of Babylon is a natural guess when you think of who was throwing his weight around, friend. But no king is named in this verse. The writer asks, “Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has ordained it?” The one he names is the Lord.
Strength is a natural guess, but the writer doesn't say it. He asks, “Why should any mortal man complain, in view of his sins?” That's the answer, baker. Strength never comes up in the verse.
